evidence.claim: If China's rare earth export controls were implemented in full, the economic value of downstream production at risk would reach USD 6.5 trillion per year for countries outside China, with the automotive sector facing the single greatest impact at over USD 3 trillion in potential direct losses, and the United States and Europe together accounting for roughly half the total.
evidence.source_name: International Energy Agency, Global Critical Minerals Outlook (Rare Earth Elements analysis), as reported the same day by Reuters via Nikkei Asia
source_excerpt: If these rare earth export controls were implemented in full, the economic value of downstream production at risk would reach USD 6.5 trillion per year for countries outside China.

The automotive sector is set to face the single greatest impact with over USD 3 trillion in potential direct losses outside China, followed by electronics and other transport (aviation, trucks and trains) sectors.

LONDON (Reuters) -- The full implementation of China's rare earth export restrictions could put $6.5 trillion of downstream production outside the country at risk, the International Energy Agency warned on Thursday.

If the controls take full effect, about $6.5 trillion of production across the automotive, high-tech, defense and energy sectors could be exposed to supply disruptions, the IEA said in its Global Critical Minerals Outlook report. The U.S. and Europe would account for nearly half of the economic impact, the report added.

evidence.claim: MOFCOM Announcement No. 62 of 2025 prohibits the export of technologies related to rare earth mining, smelting and separation, metal production, magnet manufacturing, and the recycling and utilization of secondary rare earth resources. Announcements No. 61 and 62 of 2025 are among those suspended from November 7, 2025 to November 10, 2026, and MOFCOM did not elaborate on the specific reasons for the suspension.
evidence.source_name: CIRS Group, China Temporarily Suspends Export Controls on Key Raw Materials
source_excerpt: Announcement No. 62 of 2025 of the Ministry of Commerce: Decision on Imposing Export Controls on Rare Earth-Related Technologies This announcement prohibits the export of technologies related to rare earth mining, smelting and separation, metal production, magnet manufacturing, and the recycling and utilization of secondary rare earth resources, including their carriers, as well as technologies for the assembly, debugging, maintenance, repair, and upgrading of related production lines.
The suspended announcements include MOFCOM and GAC Announcements No. 55, 56, 57, and 58 of 2025, as well as MOFCOM Announcements No. 61 and 62 of 2025.
This indicates that from November 7, 2025, to November 10, 2026, the export of these items and technologies will not be bound by the specific provisions of the previously mentioned announcements.
The Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs did not elaborate on the specific reasons for the suspension in the latest announcement.

public_reach.rationale: UNCHANGED score 2026-08-31 (fresh-evidence pass): money_at_stake was raised this run to GT_100B on the IEA's USD 6.5 trillion/year downstream-production-at-risk figure, but that figure sizes exposure at the DOWNSTREAM USER layer, the automotive, electronics, defense and energy companies that consume rare-earth inputs and are large, mostly listed firms (Toyota, GM, Lockheed, Siemens Energy and peers). That is not the same claim as this leg's question. public_reach asks how much of the money the OCCURRENCE moves lands on listed issuers as the party the occurrence's controls actually gate, i.e. who controls or captures the bottleneck, not who is exposed to it as a customer. The entities that hold the pricing power this occurrence creates or removes are the rare-earth mining, separation and magnet-manufacturing layer itself, which is exactly the narrower pool this leg was already scored against and which capture_odds' own CSIS evidence describes as still heavily China-dominated. Moving public_reach up because downstream AUTO/TECH/DEFENSE BUYERS are public would conflate exposure with capture and would be the reasoned-but-uncited inference this repo's evidence discipline forbids; the leg stays at 40 on the same confirmed listed names as before. TASTE-001 applied visibly, same scoping the candidate itself already used: this leg is scored against the separation-chemistry, magnet-manufacturing, and tooling layer Decree 62 actually controls, not against the rare-earth-miner names (MP Materials, Lynas) the rule refuses. Inside that narrower, correctly-scoped layer, one real, meaningfully-positioned listed name is confirmed by this run's own fetch: Neo Performance Materials (TSX: NEO) operates the Silmet separation plant in Estonia, described as, until recently, the only industrial-scale rare-earth separation facility operating commercially in the Western hemisphere outside Asia, and its Narva magnet-manufacturing line is ramping from 2,000 to 5,000 tonnes/year [rare-earth-mining.com, fetched and excerpted 2026-08-30]. A second listed name, Ucore Rare Metals (TSXV: UCU), is developing a Louisiana separation complex using proprietary RapidSX technology but is confirmed not yet an operating refiner at commercial scale [same source]. Score held at 40, not moved higher, because this run could not establish two things that matter to reach: whether Solvay's La Rochelle rare-earth line (shown operating in the same source's summary table, but with no ticker or listing status stated on that page) is investable at a scale that moves the leg, and what Vacuumschmelze's (VAC) ownership status actually is. CORRECTED 2026-08-30 (verification pass): the prior draft of this rationale asserted, as fact, that a rare-earth-mining.com 'company-status table' labels both Solvay and Vacuumschmelze 'privately held', and used VAC's private status as the explicit reason the score was held at 40, additionally citing a MarketScreener page as evidence that this labeling was wrong for Solvay. Directly fetching this page's full text this run (both via the fetch tool and a raw HTTP grep of its HTML) finds no 'private' or 'privately held' language anywhere on it, and no public/private company-status column at all: the page's summary table carries an operating-status column (Operating / Development / Pre-commissioning), not an ownership column, and Vacuumschmelze does not even appear as a row in that table (only Less Common Metals, which the same source separately says VAC acquired in 2012). That assertion is removed rather than repaired. The MarketScreener item is also removed: it returned HTTP 403 on both the fetch tool and a direct curl this run, and the Wayback Machine could not be reached to check an archived copy, so it is unreachable rather than merely unsupportive. This run therefore has no citable source, positive or negative, for VAC's or Solvay's public/private status, and neither is asserted. With one confirmed real operating listed name (NEO) carrying a two-plant capacity ramp, one confirmed pre-commercial listed name (UCU), and the ownership status of the sector's other most-cited capacity left genuinely unresolved by evidence gathered this run, the honest read stays a split pool rather than a clean listed pure-play set: some of it clearly reaches a brokerage account, and how much of the rest does is unknown rather than confirmed in either direction. 40 is kept as the anchor that fits 'split, with a large share of unresolved status' rather than moved to 60 (which would assert a confidence this run's evidence does not support) or down to 15 (which would assert the opposite, equally unsupported, claim that the unresolved share is state/private/sanctioned).

capture_odds.rationale: UNCHANGED score 2026-08-31 (fresh-evidence pass): the freshest dated source found this run reinforces rather than moves this leg. Modern Diplomacy's 2026-08-31 analysis of rare-earth chokepoints beyond China states plainly that 'China's 2025 licensing regime has become permanent infrastructure, and in 2026 it is tightening' [Modern Diplomacy, published and fetched 2026-08-31], which argues the same direction as the CSIS evidence already below: durable Chinese leverage over the chain, not a moat non-Chinese capacity has yet demonstrated it can hold on its own economics. Two forces cut against each other, so this sits at the middle anchor rather than being rounded toward either story. For capture: heavy-rare-earth separation and magnet-grade production at industrial scale are technically scarce, qualification-gated capabilities, not commodity processes; Neo Performance Materials' Silmet plant being described as, until recently, the only industrial-scale separation facility operating commercially outside Asia is exactly the kind of concentrated capability that normally holds price [rare-earth-mining.com, fetched and excerpted 2026-08-30]. Against capture: CSIS's one-year retrospective on these controls states that 'in the near term, supply chains remain heavily dependent on China, which continues to dominate processing, refining, and downstream manufacturing' and that 'as a result, China retains significant leverage over critical mineral supply chains' [CSIS, published 2026-04-27, fetched and excerpted 2026-08-30]. A chain segment whose surrounding ecosystem is described this way has not yet demonstrated it can hold price on its own economics once government backing is set aside, which is the pattern documented across this sector rather than a fact specific to any one ticker. Scored at 50 because the technical moat is real but its durability at market-clearing prices is exactly what this occurrence's own window (through the 2026-11-10 decision point and beyond) has not yet tested. CORRECTED 2026-08-30 (verification pass): the CSIS quote previously read 'Western supply chains ... regardless of temporary agreements'; a direct fetch and raw-HTML grep of the source this run finds neither 'Western' nor 'regardless of temporary agreements' anywhere on the page. The quote above is the source's own wording with nothing added.

timing_fit.rationale: UNCHANGED score 2026-08-31 (fresh-evidence pass): two further dated sources confirm rather than resolve the two-sided uncertainty this leg already scored. First, the mechanism itself is structurally recurring, not a one-off: President Trump described the underlying US-China rare-earth arrangement as renewed annually, 'We have a deal. Now, every year, we'll renegotiate the deal,' confirming the agreement 'would initially apply for one year' [Yahoo News/AP, fetched and excerpted 2026-08-31, dated 2025-10-30]. That supports money moving on a recurring cadence squarely inside the 2-5 year window, not a single pass/fail event. Second, independent analysis as of mid-2026 still frames the November 2026 date as genuinely open, naming 'three potential policy outcomes ahead of the November deadline: an extension of the suspension, selective reinstatement of controls targeting specific elements or end uses, and full reimposition of the October 2025 measures' [InvestorNews, fetched and excerpted 2026-08-31, dated 2026-07-17]. Neither new source moves the score: the first confirms the catalyst recurs within the horizon (supporting the existing anchor), the second confirms the two-sided uncertainty the rationale already held (arguing against moving higher). The scheduled decision point, November 10, 2026, is about 71 days past this appraisal's as_of date and squarely inside the 2-5 year horizon this repo underwrites; it is a dated, committed catalyst rather than a projected one, since the suspension's start and end dates (November 7, 2025 to November 10, 2026) are fixed by MOFCOM's own announcement rather than estimated [CIRS Group, fetched and excerpted 2026-08-30]. The broader structural story, ex-China separation and magnet-manufacturing capacity coming online (Neo's Narva ramp, Ucore's Louisiana build), plays out across exactly the 2-5 year window rather than resolving on the decision date alone. Not scored higher than 75 because the catalyst carries two-sided uncertainty the window itself will resolve rather than confirm in advance: renewal, lapse, or renegotiation are all live options as of this appraisal, and CSIS's April 2026 assessment found China's leverage over the chain undiminished a full year in, which argues for real money moving on this timeline without guaranteeing which direction the November decision pushes it. CORRECTED 2026-08-30 (verification pass): the prior draft attributed the suspension dates to a 'Busan agreement.' A direct fetch and raw-HTML grep of the cited CIRS source this run finds no mention of Busan, any summit, or any stated reason anywhere on the page; the page instead states MOFCOM 'did not elaborate on the specific reasons for the suspension.' The attribution is removed rather than replaced with an unconfirmed alternative; the dates themselves remain fully verified against the same source.
